adipose tissue: Adipose tissue stores fat as energy.
ADI refers to fat tissue, providing energy and cushioning.
Adipose tissue contains large, round fat cells.
ADI tissue appears as clusters of fat cells under the microscope.
Adipose tissue looks like clear cells with displaced nuclei due to fat.
Under the microscope, adipose tissue appears pale due to stored fat.
Adipose tissue also releases hormones like leptin.
background: BACK refers to non-specific tissue or empty space in images.
The background includes areas without specific structures.
BACK represents areas not occupied by main tissue.
Background often appears pale or unstained in images.
BACK surrounds the tissue of interest in pathology slides.
The background provides contrast to tissue structures.
In slides, the background highlights cellular details.
debris: DEB refers to cell remnants in pathology samples.
Debris includes cellular remnants or degraded material.
DEB appears as irregular dark particles in sections.
Debris can indicate cell death or tissue breakdown.
DEB is fragmented material scattered in the tissue.
Debris consists of dead cells and matrix fragments.
Debris can show signs of a previous immune response.
lymphocytes: LYM refers to lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell.
Lymphocytes are small cells with large nuclei.
LYM cells play a key role in the immune response.
Under a microscope, lymphocytes are dark-staining cells.
LYM cells are often found in clusters in immune tissues.
Lymphocytes have round shapes with dense nuclei.
Lymphocytes gather around infection or tumor sites.
mucus: MUC refers to mucus, a thick substance from mucous membranes.
Mucus serves as a protective barrier in tissues.
MUC appears as light-staining material in slides.
Mucus often indicates the presence of glands or goblet cells.
MUC represents secretions in the digestive and respiratory tracts.
Mucus traps pathogens and particles in the body.
Mucus increases during infection, acting as a barrier.
smooth muscle: MUS refers to smooth muscle, an involuntary muscle type.
Smooth muscle is found in organs like intestines and vessels.
MUS consists of spindle-shaped cells with central nuclei.
Under the microscope, smooth muscle has elongated, tapering cells.
MUS controls movements like digestion and blood flow.
Smooth muscle contracts slowly without visible striations.
Smooth muscle regulates blood flow and digestion with rhythmic contractions.
normal colon mucosa: NORM refers to healthy colon mucosa.
Normal colon mucosa consists of a single layer of epithelial cells.
NORM appears as well-organized crypts with regular lining.
In pathology, normal mucosa is used for comparison with diseased tissue.
NORM has a uniform appearance without inflammation.
Normal colon mucosa has healthy epithelial cells and crypts.
Goblet cells in normal mucosa secrete mucus for protection.
cancer-associated stroma: STR refers to the tissue surrounding a tumor.
Cancer-associated stroma contains fibroblasts and immune cells.
STR plays a role in tumor growth and progression.
In images, cancer stroma appears as dense tissue around malignant cells.
STR influences cancer behavior through signaling.
Cancer stroma is more fibrous and disorganized than normal tissue.
Stroma interacts with tumor cells, helping survival and spread.
colorectal adenocarcinoma epithelium: TUM refers to the malignant cells in colorectal cancer.
Colorectal adenocarcinoma has irregular glandular structures.
TUM appears as disorganized, abnormal formations.
TUM tissue is identified by its abnormal cell structure and growth.
TUM tissue often shows increased cell division and atypical nuclei.
Colorectal adenocarcinoma has dysplastic cells forming irregular glands.
TUM shows a loss of normal structure, with invasive growth.
